content.text: When you look up at the night sky, the thousands of points of light you see are stars, each one a massive ball of gas producing energy through nuclear fusion. Stars are the fundamental building blocks of the visible universe. They produce light and heat, they forge the chemical elements that make up planets and living things, and their life cycles shape the structure of galaxies.

Stars are not permanent. They are born, they live, and they die, each stage governed by the balance between two opposing forces: gravity pulling inward and radiation pressure pushing outward. The life story of a star depends critically on one property: its mass. A star with a mass similar to our Sun will have a very different fate from a star ten times more massive.

In this lesson, we will trace the life cycle of stars from their birth in nebulae to their eventual death as white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes. We will also explore the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, one of the most important tools in astronomy, and learn how stars create the elements that make up everything around us.

The most common fusion reaction in stars is the fusion of hydrogen into helium. Four hydrogen nuclei (protons) combine to form one helium nucleus, releasing energy in the process. This is the reaction that powers our Sun and most other stars during the main part of their lives.

The basic hydrogen fusion process involves four hydrogen nuclei (protons) combining to form one helium nucleus, releasing energy. The mass of four hydrogen nuclei is slightly greater than the mass of one helium nucleus. This mass difference is converted into energy.

A star maintains its size and shape through a delicate balance called

pulls all the matter in the star inward towards the centre, trying to compress the star.
(and gas pressure from the hot plasma) pushes outward, trying to expand the star.

When these two forces are balanced, the star is stable. If gravity were to dominate, the star would collapse. If radiation pressure were to dominate, the star would expand. During most of a star's life, these forces are in balance, and the star remains at a roughly constant size. The life cycle of a star can be understood as the story of what happens when this balance shifts.
The Life Cycle of a Star
All stars begin their lives in a

(plural: nebulae), which is a vast cloud of gas (mostly hydrogen and helium) and dust spread across many light-years of space. Nebulae are among the most beautiful objects in the universe, often appearing as colourful, glowing clouds when illuminated by nearby stars.

A nebula on its own is stable, with the gas pressure preventing it from collapsing. However, if something disturbs the nebula, such as a shockwave from a nearby supernova explosion or the gravitational influence of a passing star, regions of the nebula can begin to collapse under their own gravity.

As a region of the nebula collapses, the gas and dust are pulled together into a denser and denser clump. As the material falls inward, gravitational potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, and the gas heats up. This hot, collapsing cloud of gas is called a

A protostar is not yet a true star because it is not hot enough in its core for nuclear fusion to begin. However, as more material falls onto the protostar and the core continues to compress and heat up, the temperature rises. The protostar may take hundreds of thousands to millions of years to form, depending on its mass.
The protostar also begins to rotate and may develop a disc of material around it, from which planets may later form.
When the core temperature of the protostar reaches approximately
, hydrogen nuclei have enough kinetic energy to overcome their electrostatic repulsion and begin to fuse into helium. Nuclear fusion ignites, and the protostar becomes a true

The energy released by fusion creates an outward radiation pressure that balances the inward pull of gravity. The star reaches hydrostatic equilibrium and settles into a long, stable phase of its life. This is the
phase, and it is the longest stage in a star's life.
The main sequence phase can last:
for low-mass stars (like our Sun, which will spend about 10 billion years on the main sequence)
for very massive stars, which burn through their hydrogen fuel much more rapidly

This may seem counterintuitive: massive stars have more fuel, but they use it up much faster. A star with 10 times the mass of the Sun has roughly 10 times the fuel, but it may burn through that fuel 10,000 times faster because the higher core temperature and pressure drive fusion at a much greater rate.
During the main sequence phase, the star's luminosity (brightness) and temperature are determined primarily by its mass:

For stars with a mass roughly similar to our Sun (up to about 8 solar masses), the life cycle proceeds as follows after the main sequence:

After billions of years, the hydrogen in the core is used up. Without the energy from hydrogen fusion to support it, the core contracts under gravity and heats up further. The increased temperature in the region surrounding the core causes hydrogen in a shell around the core to begin fusing. This extra energy causes the outer layers of the star to expand enormously.
As the outer layers expand, they cool down, giving the star a reddish colour. The star has become a

. A red giant can be hundreds of times larger than the original main sequence star. When our Sun becomes a red giant in about 5 billion years, it will expand to engulf the orbits of Mercury and Venus, and possibly Earth.
Meanwhile, the core continues to heat up. When the core temperature reaches about
, helium nuclei begin to fuse into carbon and oxygen. This helium fusion provides a new source of energy, temporarily stabilising the star.

Eventually, the helium fuel in the core is also exhausted. For a Sun-like star, the core is not hot enough to fuse carbon or heavier elements. The star becomes unstable, and its outer layers are gently expelled into space, forming a beautiful expanding shell of glowing gas called a
. (Despite the name, planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets; early astronomers named them this because they appeared as small, round, planet-like discs through telescopes.)
What remains is the hot, dense core of the star, now called a

. A white dwarf has a mass comparable to the Sun but is compressed into a volume roughly the size of the Earth. A teaspoon of white dwarf material would weigh about 5 tonnes on Earth. White dwarfs have no fusion reactions occurring; they shine only because they are still very hot from the energy of their collapse. Over billions of years, a white dwarf gradually cools and fades, eventually becoming a cold, dark object sometimes called a
(though the universe is not yet old enough for any black dwarfs to have formed).

For stars with masses greater than about 8 solar masses, the life cycle takes a dramatically different and more violent path after the main sequence.

Like Sun-like stars, massive stars exhaust the hydrogen in their cores and expand. However, because of their much greater mass (and therefore stronger gravity and higher core temperatures), they expand to become
, which are far larger than red giants. A red supergiant like Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion has a diameter hundreds of times that of the Sun.

The key difference is that massive stars have enough gravitational pressure to heat their cores to the extreme temperatures needed to fuse heavier and heavier elements. After hydrogen fuses into helium, the core contracts and heats up enough to fuse helium into carbon. Then carbon fuses into neon, neon into oxygen, oxygen into silicon, and finally silicon into iron. Each stage of fusion is shorter than the last:
Helium fusion: hundreds of thousands of years
This creates an onion-like layered structure in the star's core, with the heaviest elements at the centre.

The fusion chain stops at iron. Iron is the most stable element; fusing iron nuclei does not release energy but instead requires energy to be put in. When the core becomes iron, fusion ceases, and there is no longer any outward radiation pressure to support the star. The core collapses catastrophically in a fraction of a second.
The outer layers of the star, falling inward, bounce off the incredibly dense core and are blasted outward in an enormously powerful explosion called a
. A supernova can briefly outshine an entire galaxy, releasing more energy in a few seconds than the Sun will produce in its entire lifetime.

The temperatures and pressures during a supernova are so extreme that elements heavier than iron (such as gold, silver, platinum, and uranium) are formed. These elements are scattered into space by the explosion, enriching the surrounding nebulae with heavy elements that can later be incorporated into new stars, planets, and even living organisms.

When a large number of stars are plotted on an H-R diagram, they do not scatter randomly. Instead, they fall into distinct groups:

A diagonal band running from the top-left (hot, luminous stars) to the bottom-right (cool, dim stars). About 90% of all stars fall on the main sequence. Our Sun is a main sequence star located roughly in the middle.
These are found in the upper-right region of the diagram. They are cool (red) but very luminous because of their enormous size.
These are found in the lower-left region. They are hot (white or blue-white) but very dim because of their tiny size.
The H-R diagram can be used to track the life cycle of a star. A star begins on the main sequence and, as it evolves, moves to different positions on the diagram:
A Sun-like star moves from the main sequence to the red giant region, then (after shedding its outer layers as a planetary nebula) drops down to the white dwarf region.
A massive star moves from the upper main sequence to the red supergiant region, then undergoes a supernova. The remnant (neutron star or black hole) is no longer plotted on the standard H-R diagram.

The luminosity of a star depends on two factors: its surface temperature and its surface area. Red giants are very luminous despite being relatively cool because their enormous radius more than compensates for their lower temperature. Conversely, white dwarfs are very hot but dim because they are so small.

Nucleosynthesis: How Stars Create the Elements
is the process by which new atomic nuclei are created from existing protons and neutrons. Stars are the factories of the universe, forging the elements through nuclear fusion.
The story of the elements goes like this:
created the lightest elements: hydrogen (about 75%), helium (about 25%), and trace amounts of lithium.
fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores.
fuse helium into carbon and oxygen.
continue the fusion chain, creating elements up to and including iron (element 26).

produce elements heavier than iron through a process called rapid neutron capture (the r-process). The extreme conditions during the explosion allow neutrons to be captured by atomic nuclei faster than the nuclei can decay, building up very heavy elements such as gold, platinum, and uranium.

The material ejected by supernovae and planetary nebulae enriches the interstellar medium (the gas and dust between stars). New stars and planets that form from this enriched material contain these heavier elements.

This means that the atoms in your body, the iron in your blood, the calcium in your bones, the carbon in your cells, were all forged inside stars that lived and died billions of years ago, long before our Solar System formed. As the astronomer Carl Sagan famously said, "We are made of star stuff."

Worked Example 3: Effect of Temperature on Luminosity
Two stars have the same radius, but Star X has a surface temperature of 6,000 K and Star Y has a surface temperature of 3,000 K. What is the ratio of their luminosities?
Star X is 16 times more luminous than Star Y. This shows that luminosity is very sensitive to temperature because of the fourth-power dependence.
Misconception 1: "All stars are yellow like the Sun"

Stars come in a range of colours depending on their surface temperature. The hottest stars (above 30,000 K) appear blue-white, moderately hot stars (like the Sun at about 5,800 K) appear yellow-white, and the coolest stars (below 3,500 K) appear red. The colour of a star is directly related to its temperature.
Misconception 2: "Bigger stars live longer because they have more fuel"

This is one of the most common misconceptions in astronomy. While more massive stars do have more hydrogen fuel, they consume it at a vastly greater rate. A star with 10 times the Sun's mass may live for only about 20 million years, compared to the Sun's 10 billion year main sequence lifetime. More massive stars die much younger.
Misconception 3: "A black hole is a giant vacuum cleaner that sucks everything in"

A black hole only pulls on nearby matter through gravity, just like any other object with mass. If the Sun were magically replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the planets would continue to orbit exactly as before. The difference is that a black hole is so compact that objects can get very close to it, where the gravitational field becomes extremely strong. It is only within or near the event horizon that the effects become inescapable.
Misconception 4: "The Sun will explode as a supernova"

The Sun does not have enough mass to undergo a supernova explosion. Only stars with initial masses greater than about 8 solar masses end their lives as supernovae. The Sun will end its life relatively quietly, shedding its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaving behind a white dwarf.
Misconception 5: "Stars twinkle because they are flickering"

The twinkling of stars (called scintillation) is caused by turbulence in Earth's atmosphere bending the starlight as it passes through. The stars themselves shine with a steady light. In space, above the atmosphere, stars do not twinkle.

Stars are massive balls of gas that produce energy through nuclear fusion, primarily the fusion of hydrogen into helium.
Stars maintain stability through hydrostatic equilibrium: the balance between inward gravitational force and outward radiation pressure.
All stars form from nebulae. Gravitational collapse of gas clouds produces protostars, which become main sequence stars when fusion ignites in their cores.
Sun-like stars follow the path: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf.
Massive stars follow the path: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red supergiant, supernova, neutron star or black hole.
The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots luminosity against temperature and reveals distinct groupings: the main sequence, red giants/supergiants, and white dwarfs.
Luminosity depends on both the radius and the surface temperature of a star. Larger stars and hotter stars are more luminous.
Stars create elements through nucleosynthesis. Elements up to iron are made in stellar cores; elements heavier than iron are made in supernovae.
Our Sun is a main sequence star that will eventually become a red giant and then a white dwarf.
More massive stars live shorter lives, burn hotter and brighter, and end their lives more dramatically.
A main sequence star is stable because of hydrostatic equilibrium: the inward pull of

(and gas pressure) from nuclear fusion in the core. If gravity dominates, the star contracts and heats up, increasing the fusion rate until equilibrium is restored. If radiation pressure dominates, the star expands and cools, reducing the fusion rate. This self-regulating balance keeps the star stable for the duration of its main sequence life.
